protocol.title: Node lesson 4 — The Code node
protocol.summary: A guided build: construct a scripted cell-count — two inputs feed a Code node whose returned keys become named outputs that flow live.

chips.text: you build it — nothing is pre-made

children.body: A Code node runs JavaScript when the protocol is viewed. Only import protocols from people you trust — the same rule as opening any lab macro. RM warns you on import when a protocol contains a script node.

How this lesson works. The guided tour is running in the ⬡ Nodes view on an empty canvas. Some math is awkward as one formula — a lookup, a piecewise rule, a rounding convention. The Code node takes a short JavaScript snippet instead, and you'll build one.

Two rules make it work. (1) Inputs are arguments: every variable you wire in arrives as a function argument of the same name. You'll wire cells_per_mL and volume_mL, so the script receives them by those names. (2) Outputs are the returned keys: the script returns an object, and each declared output takes the value of the matching key.

The script you'll write:
var total = cells_per_mL * volume_mL;
return { total_cells: total, millions: total / 1e6 };
Two declared outputs — total_cells and millions — pick up the two returned keys. Both become live variables the document reads: total is [!var:total_cells] cells ([!var:millions] million).

After the build, edit it live: change the script or add an output row (name it, then return that key). Move the input sliders and the outputs recompute. If a script has an error — a typo, a missing return key — that output shows the error instead of a number, and the rest of the protocol keeps working.

When to reach for it. Prefer an Equation node for ordinary arithmetic — it's simpler and safer to share. Use a Code node when the logic genuinely needs branching, arrays, or a table lookup. If you return a single number and declare a single output, you can skip the object and just return value;.

That's the full node toolkit: inputs, constants, choices, ordered sets, equations, lists, plate planners, and code. Combine them — and lean on ✨ Recipes for common patterns, or 🎓 Tours to revisit any node — to make any lab protocol calculate itself.
